full_judgment: "Thus, a hiba in such circumstances should be taken to be perfectly valid even without an express delivery of possession of the subjectmatter of the gift. By that reason, it is this Court's view that the academic exercise undertaken by the lower appellate Court with regard to finding an intention to give, and the taking of constructive possession by the donee of the suit land is well founded in law. In this regard, this Court finds no reason to accept the 'submission of the learned Advocate for the petitioner that the presumption as relied upon by the lower appellate Court in the impugned judgment, although substantiated by that Court by reference to judicial precedents, must somehow be considered negated by reason of debilitating facts as otherwise asserted by the petitioner. In further substantiation of its finding in this regard the lower appellate Court also found reason to question the plaintiff's stand taken in this case against the hiba deed without also challenging a waqf deed executed by her husband Anfar Uddin on the same date under allegedly same circumstances. It is also wondered why other transactions entered into by her husband in transferring his other properties on subsequent dates were never questioned by the plaintiff. Moreover, the said Anfar Uddin, the executor of the disputed deed, who lived for a period of four years thereafter never himself took any initiative to question or challenge the circumstances under which the gift deed is alleged to have been executed and registered. This Court is satisfied that all these issues, facts and the application of relevant law cumulatively operated in the mind of the learned Additional District Judge to correctly find for a proper execution and registration of the deed in question thereby necessitating a reversal of the trial Court's judgment and decree. This Court is further satisfied that the lower appellate Court allowed the appeal and reversed the judgment and decree of the Trial Court on a proper consideration of facts and evidence and an almost exhaustive enunciation of the law. That being the case, this Court finds no reason to interfere with that appellate decision and judgment sitting in revisional jurisdiction.
